title: Air Traffic Procedures Quiz
description: Test your knowledge of preflight planning, flight plans, NOTAMs, departure/arrival procedures, and instrument approaches from AIM Chapter 5

questions.question: What regulation requires pilots to become familiar with all available information concerning a flight before departure?
questions.explanation: 14 CFR 91.103 (Preflight Action) requires pilots to become familiar with all available information concerning that flight, including weather, fuel requirements, alternatives, and known traffic delays.

questions.question: Where can pilots access NOTAMs online?
questions.explanation: Pilots can access NOTAM information online via the FAA's Federal NOTAM System (FNS) NOTAM Search at notams.aim.faa.gov/notamSearch.

questions.question: What are the three types of preflight weather briefings?
questions.explanation: The three types of preflight briefings are: Standard (complete briefing), Abbreviated (update or supplement to previous briefing), and Outlook (planning purposes when departure is 6+ hours away).

questions.question: How long is a VFR flight plan valid after the proposed departure time?
questions.explanation: AVFR flight plan is held by FSS for 2 hours after the proposed departure time. If not activated within that time, it's automatically cancelled.

questions.question: What happens if you fail to close a VFR flight plan?
questions.explanation: Failure to close a VFR flight plan can result in costly search and rescue operations being initiated. ALWAYS close your flight plan upon arrival.

questions.question: What does FDC NOTAM stand for and what does it contain?
options: Flight Data Center - regulatory information affecting instrument procedures
questions.explanation: FDC (Flight Data Center) NOTAMs contain regulatory information such as amendments to instrument approach procedures, airspace changes, and TFRs.

questions.question: What is a CRAFT clearance?
options: A special clearance for small aircraft
A mnemonic for IFR clearance components
questions.explanation: CRAFT is a mnemonic for IFR clearance components: Clearance limit, Route, Altitude, Frequency, Transponder code.

questions.question: What altitude should you expect to maintain if communications are lost during an IFR flight?
options: The highest of: assigned, expected, or MEA
questions.explanation: Per 14 CFR 91.185, maintain the HIGHEST of: last assigned altitude, altitude ATC said to expect, or minimum en route altitude for each segment.

questions.question: What is a SID (Standard Instrument Departure)?
options: A preplanned IFR departure procedure for obstacle clearance and traffic flow
A departure clearance for jets only
questions.explanation: ASID is a preplanned IFR ATC departure procedure printed for pilot/controller use. It provides obstacle clearance and improves traffic flow.

questions.question: What does 'expect further clearance' (EFC) time mean?
options: Time to expect clearance out of holding
questions.explanation: EFC (Expect Further Clearance) time is provided when you're holding. It's the time you should expect clearance to continue. Critical for lost comm procedures.

questions.question: What is the standard holding pattern entry direction for an aircraft arriving on a heading directly opposite the outbound leg?
questions.explanation: When arriving from opposite the outbound direction (within 70° sector), use the Direct entry - turn right and fly the pattern.

questions.question: What are the three holding pattern entry procedures?
questions.explanation: The three holding pattern entries are: Direct (within 70° sector), Parallel (parallel the outbound course), and Teardrop (30° offset entry).

questions.question: What is the maximum indicated airspeed for holding patterns below 6,000 feet MSL?
questions.explanation: Maximum holding airspeeds: Below 6,000' MSL = 200 KIAS; 6,001' to 14,000' MSL = 230 KIAS; Above 14,000' MSL = 265 KIAS.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a STAR (Standard Terminal Arrival Route)?
options: To provide obstacle clearance during approach
To simplify clearance delivery and transition from en route to terminal
To separate VFR and IFR traffic
questions.explanation: STARs are preplanned IFR ATC arrival procedures that simplify clearance delivery and facilitate transition from en route to the terminal environment.

questions.question: What does DA (Decision Altitude) represent on a precision approach?
options: The altitude at which a missed approach must be initiated if visual reference is not established
The altitude of the runway threshold
questions.explanation: DA (Decision Altitude) is the altitude on a precision approach at which a missed approach must be initiated if the required visual reference to continue is not established.

questions.question: What is the difference between DA and MDA?
options: DA is for VFR, MDA is for IFR
DA is for precision approaches (you descend through it), MDA is for non-precision (you level off)
questions.explanation: DA (Decision Altitude) is used for precision approaches - you continue descent through DA if visual. MDA (Minimum Descent Altitude) is for non-precision - you level off and can only descend further when runway environment is in sight.

questions.question: What visual references are required to descend below DA/MDA?
options: The runway environment (threshold, markings, lights, VASI, etc.)
questions.explanation: To descend below DA/MDA, pilot must have runway environment in sight: threshold, threshold markings/lights, REIL, VASI, touchdown zone, runway or its markings, or ALS (if can identify threshold).

questions.question: What is the Final Approach Fix (FAF) on a non-precision approach?
options: The point where you begin timing
The fix from which the final approach segment begins
The point where you contact tower
questions.explanation: The FAF is the fix from which the final approach to the runway begins. It's identified by a Maltese cross on the profile view. Timing for missed approach starts here.

questions.question: What does the term 'procedure turn' refer to?
options: A course reversal maneuver to establish inbound on the final approach course
A turn at the missed approach point
questions.explanation: A procedure turn is a maneuver to reverse direction and establish the aircraft inbound on the intermediate or final approach course. Normally remain within 10 NM.

questions.question: When is a procedure turn NOT authorized?
options: When 'NoPT' is shown on the chart
When radar vectors are provided to final
questions.explanation: A procedure turn is not required/authorized when: 'NoPT' is shown, radar vectors to final are provided, holding is in lieu of PT, timed approach, or direct approach via feeder route.

questions.question: What is a circling approach?
options: A visual maneuver to land on a runway not aligned with the approach
questions.explanation: A circling approach is a visual maneuver conducted after completing an instrument approach to land on a runway that is not aligned with the final approach course (greater than 30° offset).

questions.question: What is the missed approach point (MAP)?
options: The point at which a missed approach must be initiated if visual reference not established
questions.explanation: The MAP is the point at which a missed approach procedure is executed if visual reference is not established. It varies by approach type (DA for precision, timing/DME for non-precision).

questions.question: What should you do immediately upon initiating a missed approach?
options: Fly the published missed approach procedure
questions.explanation: Upon going missed, immediately climb and fly the published missed approach procedure unless given alternate instructions by ATC. Advise ATC as soon as practical.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the Visual Descent Point (VDP)?
options: A point from which a normal descent can be made to the runway
questions.explanation: The VDP is a defined point on non-precision approaches from which a normal (approximately 3°) descent from MDA to touchdown can be made. Shown as 'V' on approach plate.

questions.question: What does 'vectors to final' mean?
options: ATC radar guidance to intercept the final approach course
questions.explanation: 'Vectors to final' means ATC is providing radar headings to guide you to intercept the final approach course. No procedure turn is authorized.

questions.question: When can you cancel IFR with ATC?
options: Anytime you're in VFR conditions (Class A excluded)
questions.explanation: You may cancel IFR anytime you're in VFR conditions, except in Class A airspace (IFR required). Canceling releases the airspace for other IFR traffic.

questions.question: What is a contact approach?
options: An approach flown to a specific runway
A pilot-requested approach to an airport with at least 1 SM visibility while clear of clouds
An approach using ground contact only
The same as a visual approach
questions.explanation: A contact approach must be requested by the pilot (can't be assigned). Requires: at least 1 SM flight visibility, clear of clouds, and reasonably expect to continue to destination.

questions.question: What is required for ATC to assign a visual approach?
options: Pilot reports airport or preceding aircraft in sight with ceiling at/above 1,000 feet and visibility 3+ miles
IFR flight plan must be closed first
questions.explanation: For a visual approach: ceiling at or above 1,000 feet and visibility 3+ miles at the airport. Pilot must report airport in sight or preceding aircraft in sight (if following).

questions.question: What NOTAMs are NOT provided in a standard briefing unless specifically requested?
questions.explanation: FSS briefers do not provide FDC NOTAM information for special instrument approach procedures unless specifically requested. Pilots authorized to use special IAPs must request these.

questions.question: What is the recommended minimum altitude for VFR flight at night in mountainous terrain?
options: At or above the MEA shown on charts
questions.explanation: When flying VFR at night, especially in mountainous terrain, maintain an altitude at or above the minimum en route altitude (MEA) shown on charts. Don't rely on eyes alone.
